analysis.one_liner: Charges polluters a rising fee on fossil fuels and methane, returning most revenue to lower- and middle-income families.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in June 2021, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge a fee of $54 per ton of carbon dioxide on coal, petroleum products, and natural gas starting in 2023, rising each year and jumping higher if the country misses its emissions targets. It would also charge oil, gas, and coal companies for methane leaked from their supply chains, and factories near low-income or minority neighborhoods for smog-causing pollution. Most of the money would go back to taxpayers as rebates — $800 per person, $1,600 per couple, plus $300 per dependent — with additional funds for weatherization, job training, and five years of wage and health coverage for coal workers whose plants close.
analysis.who_benefits: Lower- and middle-income taxpayers receive annual rebates of $800 per individual ($1,600 joint) plus $300 per dependent, phasing out above $75,000 of income ($150,000 joint). Coal workers laid off from closing mines or plants would get five years of wage replacement and continued health coverage. Every state and tribe would get a share of $10 billion a year for energy-efficiency help, job training, and cleanup of fossil fuel damage. Communities near major industrial polluters would benefit from new fees on soot, ozone-forming, and acid-rain pollution, plus public reporting of the emissions data.

how_it_helps.text: Every eligible taxpayer would receive $800 ($1,600 for joint returns) plus $300 per dependent per year, and the rebate is refundable, meaning even families that owe no income tax would get it.
The fee starts at $54 per ton of CO2 in 2023, rises about 6 percent plus inflation each year, and climbs an additional 5 percent in any year the country exceeds its cumulative emissions target.
Coal workers who lose their jobs when a mine or plant closes would receive wage replacement for 60 months, adjusted for inflation, plus health coverage matching what their employer paid.

Factories near low-income communities, communities of color, or tribal lands would pay per-pound fees on nitrogen oxides, fine particles, and sulfur dioxide, with continuous monitoring and monthly public reporting.
Imported goods would face an equalizing fee based on the carbon used to make them abroad, so the domestic fee would not simply push manufacturing overseas.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers, importers, and chemical makers would bear the fees directly. Some of the cost would reach households through higher prices for gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity; the rebates are designed to more than offset that for most families below the income phase-out thresholds, while higher-income households absorb the difference without a rebate.

drawbacks.text: Households earning above the phase-out thresholds ($75,000 single, $150,000 joint, $112,500 head of household) would pay higher energy prices with no rebate to offset them, and even below those lines, heavy energy users could see their rebate consumed by price increases.
Gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity prices would rise beginning in 2023, before or alongside the rebate checks, so some households would face higher costs at the pump and on bills in the interim.
Farming operations are exempted from the fee on non-combustion greenhouse gas emissions, leaving a major methane source outside the charge.

The methane fee depends on operators accurately self-reporting leaks and venting across their supply chains, with third-party verification rules still to be written by regulators, so the amounts collected could turn heavily on implementation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design follows the 'carbon dividend' model: the fees concentrate on the largest fossil fuel companies, and the rebates return the money in a way that most favors lower- and middle-income households, who use less energy than the wealthy. The strongest honest objection is timing and distribution — higher prices arrive at the pump and on utility bills immediately, the rebate arrives through the tax system, and any household above the income phase-out pays in full. The bill also leaves a large gap, notably the farm exemption, and its methane provisions lean on self-reporting. On balance, the benefits to households and coal communities outweigh the acknowledged interim costs for most families, but the burdens are real for those above the rebate limits.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on June 16, 2021, joined by five Senate Democrats as original sponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
Nine Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.
The action history shows no further steps after the committee referral — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill died at the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers, importers, and industrial polluters are better off because no carbon or pollution fee was ever enacted. Coal communities and climate-exposed households gained nothing, since the worker and community assistance died with the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers; no fee was ever enacted

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.role: U.S. Senator from Rhode Island; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its sponsorship.

for.name: Sens. Schatz, Heinrich, Gillibrand, Murphy, and Reed
for.what_they_did: Joined the introduction of the bill on June 16, 2021.

against.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: His committee took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing or markup was scheduled in the entire Congress.

against.name: Fossil fuel industry
against.role: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers and trade groups
against.what_they_did: Have a long record of lobbying against carbon pricing measures; the bill's fees would fall directly on their products.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican signed on; with 50 Republicans in the chamber, the bill's tax mechanism would also have faced steep odds in the Finance Committee even if it had advanced.

industries.industry: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers
industries.note: The bill charges them $54 per ton of CO2 on their products, rising yearly, plus fees on methane vented or leaked across their supply chains. Their interest in the bill's failure runs against the public rebate and cleanup programs that died with it.

industries.industry: Fluorinated greenhouse gas makers (refrigerants and industrial gases)
industries.note: The bill would have phased in a full carbon-equivalent fee on these extremely potent gases by 2032, on top of the general fossil fuel fees.

industries.industry: Industrial facilities near low-income and minority neighborhoods
industries.note: Major sources within a mile of an environmental justice community would owe annual per-pound fees on smog, soot, and acid-rain pollution, with mandatory continuous monitoring and fines for false reporting.

They would pay higher fuel costs, but the bill refunds fees on exports and imposes equalizing fees on carbon-intensive imports, shielding them from foreign competition — a trade protection bundled with the climate fee.

industries.industry: Renewable energy and carbon capture industries
industries.note: A rising fossil fuel fee would make clean power more price-competitive, and companies that capture and permanently store carbon dioxide would earn refunds per ton.
